params.question: A fracture that heals without residual disability but requires ten weeks of traction does not warrant structured prognosis counselling.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Not quite. The video identifies fractures needing prolonged bed rest as one of the four categories requiring prognosis counselling, regardless of long-term disability. The social, financial, and medical complications of weeks of immobilisation — including pressure sores, blood clots, and muscle wasting — make early counselling essential.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well done. Fractures requiring prolonged immobilisation are one of the four categories that need structured prognosis counselling, even when full recovery is expected. Weeks of traction carry real costs — job loss, family disruption, pressure sores, and blood clots — and the patient must be prepared for these early.

params.question: A 55-year-old woman is diagnosed with osteosarcoma of the proximal tibia. She asks whether amputation will definitely cure her. What is the most appropriate counselling response?

answers.text: "Amputation will guarantee a complete cure, so you should not worry."

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Offering certainty about survival contradicts the counselling principle for bone tumours. The video emphasises reporting survival as probabilities, never certainties, and never offering false reassurance.

answers.text: "I will present the survival probabilities for both limb-salvage surgery and amputation so we can make an informed decision together."

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The video instructs using the SPIKES protocol, presenting both limb-salvage and amputation as legitimate options with their risks, and reporting survival figures as probabilities — never certainties.

answers.text: "We should not discuss survival statistics as they will only cause unnecessary distress."

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Withholding prognostic information contradicts the SPIKES framework. Bone tumour counselling requires full disclosure, including survival probabilities for each treatment option, delivered with empathy.

answers.text: "The oncologist will explain everything later; it is not the orthopaedic team's responsibility."

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The video makes clear that the surgeon must disclose the diagnosis and discuss both limb-salvage and amputation. Deferring entirely to another specialist delays the patient's understanding and violates the disclosure obligation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the bone tumour counselling section. The key principles are: use the SPIKES protocol in full, explain both limb-salvage and amputation as legitimate options, and report survival figures as probabilities, never as certainties.
Excellent. You correctly applied the bone tumour counselling principle: use the SPIKES protocol, present both surgical options honestly, and convey survival as probabilities — never guarantees.

interactions.label: In compartment syndrome, which clinical sign is the earliest and most reliable i

params.question: In compartment syndrome, which clinical sign is the earliest and most reliable indicator, even when distal pulses are still palpable?

answers.text: Paralysis of the affected muscles

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Paralysis is a late sign indicating that irreversible nerve and muscle damage has already occurred. Waiting for paralysis means missing the critical window for fasciotomy.

answers.text: Pulselessness distal to the injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pulselessness is a late finding. The video explicitly warns that a palpable pulse does NOT rule out compartment syndrome — do not wait for this sign.

answers.text: Visible pallor of the affected limb

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pallor is a late sign that may not be present in early compartment syndrome. The limb may appear normal in the early stages, making this an unreliable early indicator.

answers.text: Pain on passive stretching of the involved muscles

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The video identifies pain on passive stretch as the earliest and most reliable sign of compartment syndrome. Crucially, pulselessness and paralysis appear late — a normal pulse does not exclude the diagnosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the six P's of compartment syndrome taught in this section. Among them, pain on passive stretching is the earliest and most reliable sign. Pulselessness and paralysis appear late and indicate that tissue damage has already occurred.

Well done. Pain on passive stretch is the single most important early warning sign of compartment syndrome. Among the six P's, pulselessness and paralysis are late — never wait for them before acting.

interactions.label: Why is below-knee amputation considered the most functional level of lower limb

params.question: Why is below-knee amputation considered the most functional level of lower limb amputation?

answers.text: It preserves the knee joint, keeping energy expenditure low and maintaining proprioception

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Preserving the knee joint dramatically reduces the energy cost of walking compared with above-knee amputation and maintains the patient's sense of joint position (proprioception), both critical for rehabilitation.

answers.text: It allows direct weight-bearing on the stump without any prosthesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Direct weight-bearing without a prosthesis is a feature of Syme's amputation, which preserves the heel pad for end-bearing. Below-knee amputation requires a prosthetic socket for walking.

answers.text: It has the shortest surgical time and lowest complication rate of all levels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The functional advantage of below-knee amputation is unrelated to operative duration. Its superiority lies in preserving the knee joint, not in surgical simplicity.

answers.text: It is the only amputation level compatible with modern prosthetic feet

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Modern prosthetic feet can be fitted at several amputation levels, including Syme's and through-knee. The advantage of below-knee lies specifically in knee preservation, not prosthetic foot compatibility.

overallFeedback.feedback: Revisit the amputation levels section. Below-knee amputation is the most functional because it preserves the knee joint — this reduces the energy cost of walking and maintains proprioception, both of which are critical for successful prosthetic rehabilitation.

Excellent. The key trade-off in amputation surgery is healing certainty versus preserved function. Below-knee amputation offers the best functional outcome because it keeps the knee joint intact, reducing energy costs and preserving proprioception.

interactions.label: Why does a below-knee amputee need prosthetic socket refitting at three, six, an

params.question: Why does a below-knee amputee need prosthetic socket refitting at three, six, and twelve months after the initial fitting?

answers.text: Because prosthetic materials degrade with regular use and require scheduled replacement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Socket refitting is driven by biological changes in the stump, not by material wear. The socket itself remains structurally sound for much longer than the refitting interval.

answers.text: Because the patient's walking pattern stabilises at three-month intervals, requiring socket adjustment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While gait does improve with training, the reason for refitting is the changing stump shape. A poorly fitting socket actually impedes gait improvement rather than the other way around.

answers.text: Because the stump continues to change shape over twelve to eighteen months as swelling reduces and tissues remodel

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The residual limb undergoes progressive volume changes as post-operative oedema resolves and muscle atrophy occurs, requiring periodic socket adjustments to maintain proper fit, comfort, and function.

answers.text: Because government prosthetic service protocols mandate fixed review intervals regardless of clinical need

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Refitting is based on the biological fact that the stump reshapes over twelve to eighteen months. It is a clinical necessity driven by anatomy, not merely a bureaucratic protocol.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: the stump changes shape for twelve to eighteen months after amputation as swelling reduces and tissues remodel. This biological process is why refitting at three, six, and twelve months is standard practice — it is not about material wear or policy mandates.

Well done. Counselling patients about the expected schedule of socket refitting — and explaining that stump shape changes are normal — helps set realistic expectations and prevents complications from a poorly fitting prosthesis.

interactions.label: A 65-year-old diabetic patient's below-knee amputation wound has healed well at

params.question: A 65-year-old diabetic patient's below-knee amputation wound has healed well at six weeks. What is the most appropriate next step in the rehabilitation programme?

answers.text: Fit the definitive prosthesis immediately and begin community walking training

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The definitive prosthesis is fitted at three to six months, not at six weeks. At this early stage, the stump is still changing shape rapidly, so a preparatory prosthesis is used first to allow adjustment.

answers.text: Fit a preparatory prosthesis and begin graded mobilisation — standing, then stepping, then walking

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Between weeks six and twelve, once healing is solid, a preparatory prosthesis is fitted and the patient begins graded mobilisation. Expect high fatigue during this phase — that is normal, not a sign of failure.

answers.text: Continue compression bandaging and bed rest for another six weeks before any prosthetic fitting

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Once the wound has healed, delaying prosthetic fitting wastes valuable rehabilitation time and risks muscle atrophy and joint stiffness. The next phase is a preparatory prosthesis with graded mobilisation.

answers.text: Discharge with crutches and schedule the first prosthetic fitting at six months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Delaying prosthetic fitting to six months results in stump muscle atrophy, joint contracture, and loss of motivation. Early fitting with a preparatory prosthesis between six and twelve weeks is the standard of care.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the staged rehabilitation timeline. The programme has three phases: pre-prosthetic (0–6 weeks — wound healing and compression), preparatory prosthesis (6–12 weeks — graded mobilisation), and definitive prosthesis (3–6 months — community walking and functional training).
Excellent. You correctly applied the rehabilitation timeline: once the wound heals at around six weeks, a preparatory prosthesis begins the graded transition from bed to standing to walking.
